closest_prior_work.citation: Qu et al. (2026). Utilizing Earth Foundation Models to Enhance the Simulation Performance of Hydrological Models with AlphaEarth Embeddings. arXiv:2601.01558. AEF similarity identifies hydrologically relevant donor basins and improves prediction in ungauged basins.
closest_prior_work.difference: This paper tests embedding-distance donor selection for basin streamflow, whereas the reviewed paper tests same-vegetation wetland reference screening against inventory water-regime labels.

closest_prior_work.citation: Liu et al. (2026). Geospatial Foundation Embeddings as Transferable Catchment Descriptors. Geophysical Research Letters. The study evaluates AlphaEarth and StefaLand embeddings as catchment descriptors across temporal and spatial generalization tasks.
closest_prior_work.difference: That work evaluates catchment descriptors for rainfall-runoff prediction; this paper evaluates whether a single embedding distance improves pairwise wetland matching beyond terrain and surface-water covariates.

closest_prior_work.citation: Ryan et al. (2026). Streamlining Wetland Vegetation Mapping with AlphaEarth Embeddings. Remote Sensing, 18(2), 293. AlphaEarth embeddings achieved accuracy comparable to traditional wetland-mapping workflows.
closest_prior_work.difference: Ryan et al. classify wetland vegetation, while this paper holds vegetation subclass fixed and asks whether embedding distance helps match a separate water-regime label.

closest_prior_work.citation: Assessment of Inundation Dynamics in Nebraska Using AlphaEarth Foundations Embeddings (2026), Research Square. The study uses AlphaEarth embeddings for regional-scale surface-water inundation mapping.
closest_prior_work.difference: This close inundation-mapping work is not discussed in the paper; it classifies inundation rather than testing incremental reference-site matching against an explicit hydrological baseline.

closest_prior_work.citation: Brown et al. (2025). AlphaEarth Foundations: An embedding field model for accurate and efficient global mapping from sparse label data. arXiv:2507.22291. Prior summaries note strong transfer across land-cover, crop, tree and biophysical tasks.
closest_prior_work.difference: Brown et al. provide broad foundation-model benchmarks; this paper provides a narrower controlled increment test for wetland inventory-regime matching with permutation, seed and constant-feature controls.

main_issues.issue: Construct and temporal validity are weak: the endpoint is agreement with interpreted NWI labels, mostly from source imagery dated 2014 or earlier, compared mainly with 2024 embeddings, with no field hydroperiod, water-source or restoration-outcome validation.

The equal-window primary estimand is highly fragile: two windows with only 19 accepted queries supply 76.8% of the AlphaEarth change, one window contributes a one-error difference among five accepted queries, and the pooled AlphaEarth effect is only -0.67 percentage points.

The headline own-screen comparison mixes reference ranking with method-specific query selection; on the fixed hydrological screen the AlphaEarth ranking component falls to -0.52 percentage points, so the result is not mainly better references for the same queries.

Attribution remains informal: only three planned permutations and limited seed repetitions are used, there is no formal permutation distribution, later six-seed means lack matched permutations, and adding a feature changes random-forest random draws even when the added column is constant.

Conclusions are learner- and baseline-dependent: the primary hydrological pair forest does not beat geographic nearest reference on the window mean, boosted trees change the comparison, and an all-feature physical forest reaches 32.78% mismatch, below the primary augmented forests.

The manuscript reports an excessive number of exploratory panels, years, sampling operators, allocations, transformations and boundary checks without independent confirmation, making the evidentiary hierarchy hard to sustain despite careful labelling.

Reproducibility from the paper alone is incomplete: it points to a local research directory and internal file paths rather than a persistent public repository or DOI in the manuscript, and the exact window locations and full 30-covariate specification are not fully recoverable from the PDF.

Scope is narrow and the physical baseline is incomplete: 12 convenience US windows, restricted NWI codes and polygon-derived samples, closed three-class labels, and no explicit SAR-derived inundation predictor limit claims about wetland hydrology generally.

research_question.predictable_reason: Some label information in embeddings was predictable given prior embedding-prediction work, but the size of any increment over explicit terrain and surface-water covariates and the dominance of seed and tiny-window variation were not predictable in detail.
research_question.question: Does adding annual AlphaEarth or TESSERA embedding distance to terrain, optical surface-water and drainage covariates improve same-vegetation wetland reference screening for matching National Wetlands Inventory water-regime labels at fixed screening coverage?

score_reasons.clarity: The background and caveats are careful, but the abstract and 36-page results are overloaded with exploratory conditions and dense, sometimes malformed, appendix tables.
score_reasons.correctness: The central negative conclusion is cautiously supported by permutations, seed checks, fixed-screen analyses and alternative learners, although the qualification rule is descriptive rather than a formal test and uncertainty remains substantial.
score_reasons.generality: Results come from 12 convenience windows, restricted NWI classes, inventory-derived polygons and mostly old labels, so they do not generalize to field hydroperiod, national wetland populations or operational reference selection.
score_reasons.novelty: The exact wetland inventory-regime screening test and its null controls appear new within the searched range, but embedding similarity for hydrological analogue and donor selection was already established.
score_reasons.usefulness: It usefully raises the evidence bar for embedding-based matching and exposes seed, selection and measurement-support artefacts, but it provides no validated operational improvement for practitioners.
score_reasons.verifiability: Hyperparameters, seeds, spatial design and many diagnostics are reported in unusual detail, but key data, code and supplementary artefacts are referenced through non-persistent local paths rather than accessible identifiers in the paper.

strengths: Label-masked, spatially separated comparison with candidates restricted to the same window and vegetation subclass and with both pair-model and category-model hydrological baselines.

Exceptionally transparent diagnostics, including embedding permutations, independent scalars, constant columns, multiple seeds, alternative learners, fixed-query screens and leave-one-window-out checks.
Clear separation between exploratory label prediction, prespecified screening performance and unmeasured field hydrological validity.
Useful measurement-support analysis showing that polygon-wide sampling can change both embedding and physical-covariate comparisons, not only the satellite result.
review.summary: This is an unusually transparent but greatly overextended negative diagnostic of whether AlphaEarth or TESSERA distances add wetland reference-screening value beyond 30 terrain, surface-water and drainage covariates. The prespecified equal-window gains of -2.95 and -3.72 percentage points are not established as attributable embedding effects because permutations and seed variation are comparable, intervals often cross zero, pooled effects are smaller, and tiny windows dominate the AlphaEarth result. The paper correctly distinguishes predicting inventory labels from improving reference choice for identical queries and from field hydroperiod validity, but its narrow, temporally mismatched inventory endpoint, fragile primary estimand, learner-dependent baseline and lack of a persistent reproducibility link prevent a stronger verdict.
